answers.justification: Ashgrove and Millbrook inflows together stayed flat (5,060 vs 5,075 m³/day, C4) while Ashgrove rose and Millbrook fell by the same amount within the same minutes (E2, C4). That means the extra water went into Millbrook's network, not out of an Ashgrove main. The acoustic survey also found only 0.4 L/s of leaks (C2), and the model never tested other draw-off points (C13).

At S1, a sustained 8.6 L/s step with no rise in household use (C7, C12), a steady PRV (E4, C1) and closed boundary valves (E5, C6) points toward a burst. However, the Station Road works next door started the same day (E3), and the boundary check only covered recorded links (E5), so a transfer into Millbrook was still an equally live rival.
PRV outlet pressure held at 3.97–4.03 bar throughout, including after 9 Sept, while the valve opened further to pass more flow (E4). The controller log shows no alarms or setpoint changes (C1).

The method statement and site diary describe an 80 mm overland hose from Ashgrove hydrant AG-417 to Millbrook, charged on 9 Sept and still connected on 3 Oct (C5). Millbrook inflow fell by about 8.4 L/s at 06:38–06:44 as Ashgrove's rose 8.6 L/s at 06:40 (C4, E2), the combined inflow balanced (C4), and Millbrook's no-water calls stopped by 06:50 (C11).

At S1 the boundary valves were sealing and network control had no recorded cross-feeds (E5, C6). That check could not rule out an unrecorded link, and the adjoining Millbrook works began on the day of the step (E3), so H3 was live but unestablished.

Smart-meter household night use stayed at 2.0 L/h (C7). The heatwave raised only daytime demand and left night flows in the other DMAs within ±0.4 L/s (C12, E2), and Ashgrove's raised flow continued after the heat ended (E2).

Control had no record of the link and the shift log never mentions it (E5, C8). But control was taken up with the Northfield burst, calls were not being recorded, the duty controller has not been interviewed (C8), and the diary's claim that control 'ok'd' the link was written up after the fact (C5). The evidence does not settle the question either way.

The timing matches to the minute (C4, E2, C5, C11). There is a clear mechanism: a hose from AG-417 feeding Millbrook (C5). The two meters move in opposite directions while the combined inflow stays flat (C4), which rules out the main rival, a burst inside Ashgrove.
The service was on 5 Sept but the drop began on 9 Sept (E1, E2). The outlet held its 4.0 bar setpoint the whole time, with no alarms or overrides logged (E4, C1).
Fenwick Fields was fully connected by 29 Aug, well before the 9 Sept step (C3, E3), and its design night demand is only 0.05 L/s against an 8.6 L/s step (C3).

Removing the documented hose link (C5) after confirming the Station Road main is back in service (C5 diary, 27 Sept) treats the most likely cause. Checking both district meters and the Beacon Hill logger afterwards will confirm or rule out H3 cheaply, before the £84,500 possession is booked (C14).

A setting of 4.8 bar breaks the PM-7 cap of 4.2 bar, which was set after 14 cast-iron bursts at 4.6 bar (E4). It would push even more water through the link into Millbrook (C5) without fixing the cause.

Whether the contractor failed to tell control is unresolved: the diary claims control 'ok'd' the link, the call recorder was offline and the duty controller has not been interviewed (C5, C8). A non-conformance now could penalise the wrong party.
Customers were already texted on 16 and 29 Sept and a web notice is kept updated (E6), so another letter is reasonable but adds little and is not among the best next actions.

The flat combined inflow (C4), the documented and still-connected hose link (C5) and the matching timing (E2, C11) are enough to justify removing the link (A1). The decision is low-risk and reversible, and recovery checks will verify it.

ambiguousItems: S02: at S1 a careful reviewer could answer 'supported', since a sustained step with demand, the PRV, Fenwick Fields and recorded boundary links all excluded points to a burst. 'Unknown' rests on the same-day Millbrook works start being an unexcluded rival.
S05: at S1, 'contradicted' is defensible on the strength of the sealed valves and the no-record check (E5), against 'unknown' because of the timing coincidence with the works (E3).
S14: 'acceptable' vs 'preferred'/'premature'. A further letter is redundant given the texts and web notice already in place (E6), but it is not harmful.
caseProblems: C5's title ('Station Road main renewal ... method statement, permit and contractor site diary') strongly signals that this item is decisive, but it does not state the answer outright.

Minor gap in C4/C5: Millbrook's inflow did not recover after its own feed was recommissioned on 27 Sept. This is plausible because Ashgrove's higher pressure would keep driving water through the still-connected hose, but the case does not say so explicitly.

C13 tested only two nodes. Hydrant AG-417 on Kestrel Road sits at the RC end, which explains why RC-3 fitted the data. This is internally consistent, but the consultant's limitation note carries a lot of the weight of the trap.

rulings.explanation: Taking the S1 evidence only, the key's case is strong. E2 shows a sudden, lasting step. E4/C1 rule out the PRV. E3/C3/C7/C12 rule out demand. E5/C6 show the mapped boundary valves are sealing, and control says no temporary links are on record. On that reading 'supported' follows. But H1 is supported only if the transfer rival is excluded, and that exclusion rests on 'nothing on record'. Records are not physical evidence about a temporary link. E3 puts a main renewal in the adjoining district starting the same day as the step, under a permit that requires continuity arrangements. A careful analyst can reasonably say that the records check excludes only notified links, so a transfer stays as live as a burst. That gives 'unknown'. The blind solver reached 'unknown' even after the earlier revision added 'hose or hydrant links' to E5. So the tension is real and not a misreading: an absence of records cannot rule out an unnotified link when the same-day coincidence is on the page. Both answers are defensible.
rulings.fix: Rekey S02 to 'unknown' and make the records check explicitly non-exclusionary. In E5, after 'none were on record', add: 'Control pointed out that their record lists only arrangements already filed with them. The permit-to-work agreement field for works on PTW-2291 is completed only at close-out, so a link agreed or set up on site would not show yet.' The S1 picture then stays 'burst or transfer, undecided', and the stage revision to 'contradicted' via C4/C5 still holds. To keep 'supported' instead, S1 evidence would need a physical exclusion of a hose, and that would conflict with the ground truth.

rulings.explanation: This is the mirror of S02. 'Contradicted' rests on two things: (a) the four mapped valves were physically confirmed sealing, and (b) control had no temporary links on record. (a) covers only mapped pipe connections. (b) is an absence of records, not an observation. E3 shows works in the adjoining district starting on 9 Sept, the same day as the step, under a permit condition about continuity arrangements. That is a positive pointer toward a temporary cross-feed. The key's own S07 rationale accepts that 'not on record' does not mean nothing was arranged, although it relies on S2 evidence (C8) to say so. A careful S1 analyst can therefore read the evidence as counting against H3 ('contradicted'). They can equally read it as leaving H3 live but unestablished ('unknown'). Both readings are defensible.
rulings.fix: Rekey S05 to 'unknown' and apply the same E5 edit as for S02, stating that control's record holds only arrangements already filed and that the PTW-2291 agreement field is filled in only at close-out. With that edit, nothing at S1 physically excludes a temporary non-pipe link, and the same-day adjoining works keep H3 live. 'Unknown' becomes the only defensible answer, and C4/C5 still move it to 'supported' at S2.

rulings.explanation: A4 is not hypothesis-dependent, so 'premature' does not fit. It does not suppress information or disable a control, so 'harmful' does not fit. 'Preferred' would need it to be among the best next actions. E6 records that every Beacon Hill and Ridgeway customer was already texted on 16 and 29 Sept and that a web notice is kept up to date, and A4 is worded as a 'further letter'. It adds little and restores no pressure, while A1 directly fixes the cause. Customers have been below the service level for weeks (E1), so communicating is reasonable and harmless. 'Acceptable' is the only answer that fits.
